config.title: Container query units (cqw, cqh)

intro.title: Container query units (cqw, cqh)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple card component that adapts its text size and padding based on the size of its container, not the entire screen. You will learn how to use the new CSS container query units, specifically cqw (container query width) and cqh (container query height), to create responsive designs. These units allow you to size elements relative to the dimensions of their nearest container with a defined containment context, making your components more modular and reusable. By the end, you'll understand how to apply these units in your CSS to make elements scale dynamically within their parent containers.
intro.usecase: Container query units like cqw and cqh are essential for building responsive components that adapt to their immediate container rather than the entire viewport. In real applications, you'll use these units to create flexible dashboard widgets that resize properly within their grid cells, or form controls that maintain proportional spacing within different-sized panels. For example, a filter sidebar in an e-commerce site can use cqw units to scale its input fields and buttons based on the sidebar's current width, ensuring consistent usability whether the sidebar is expanded or collapsed. This approach is particularly valuable for complex interfaces like admin panels, where nested components need independent responsive behavior without relying on global viewport dimensions.

objectives: Apply container query units (cqw, cqh) to style elements based on container dimensions
Configure container-type properties to establish query containers
Implement responsive typography using cqw and cqh units
Construct layout components that adapt using container query units
Manipulate element sizing with container-relative units instead of viewport units
Integrate cqw/cqh units with existing CSS properties like padding and margin
Update existing viewport-based designs to use container query units

steps.title: Create HTML structure with container and card elements
steps.instruction: Create an HTML file with a container div containing multiple card divs.
steps.hint: Start with a basic HTML structure. Inside the body, add a div with class 'container'. Inside that container, add three divs with class 'card'.

steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Container Query Units</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add your container and card elements here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a complete HTML file with a container div and three card divs inside it, ready to be styled with CSS container query units.
successCriteria: The HTML file contains a div with class 'container' and three divs with class 'card' inside it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have exactly one container div with class 'container' and three card divs with class 'card' inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the required structure. Please create an HTML file with a container div containing three card divs.

steps.title: Add basic styling to the container and cards
steps.instruction: Open the styles.css file and add CSS rules to style the container and cards with width, height, background colors, and basic spacing.
steps.hint: Start by targeting the container element (you'll need to add a class or ID to it in the HTML later) and set its width. Then style the cards with dimensions, background colors, and margin/padding.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file will have initial styling rules for the container and card elements, establishing their visual foundation.
successCriteria: CSS file contains rules for container width and card dimensions, colors, and spacing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure to include rules for both container width and card dimensions/colors/spacing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS file doesn't contain the expected styling rules. Try adding rules for container width and card dimensions, colors, and spacing.

steps.title: Define container-type property on the container
steps.instruction: Add the CSS property `container-type: inline-size;` to the `.container` selector to make it a query container for container query units.
steps.hint: This property tells the browser that the container's width (inline-size) should be used as a reference for container query units like cqw.
steps.expectedOutcome: The container element will be established as a query container, enabling the use of container query units (cqw, cqh) for its child elements.
successCriteria: The `.container` selector has the property `container-type: inline-size;`
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added `container-type: inline-size;` to the `.container` selector.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container needs the `container-type: inline-size;` property to become a query container for container query units.

steps.title: Introduce container query with cqw unit for font size
steps.instruction: Add a container query to the .card class that sets the font-size of card titles to 5cqw when the container width is at least 400px.
steps.hint: Use the @container rule with a min-width condition, then target a .card-title element inside to apply font-size: 5cqw.
steps.expectedOutcome: The .card class will have a container query that makes card titles scale with container width using cqw units.
successCriteria: A container query with @container (min-width: 400px) is added, and inside it, .card-title has font-size: 5cqw.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both the @container rule with the correct condition and the .card-title selector with font-size: 5cqw.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container query is missing or incorrect. Check the syntax and ensure you're using cqw units for the font-size.

steps.title: Apply cqw unit to padding
steps.instruction: Inside the existing container query, add a rule to adjust the card's padding using cqw units. Use a value like 2cqw.
steps.hint: Add a padding property inside the @container rule, using cqw as the unit. For example: padding: 2cqw;
steps.expectedOutcome: The card's padding will now respond to the container's width, using container query units.
successCriteria: The container query includes a padding property with cqw units (e.g., padding: 2cqw;)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you added the padding property inside the container query with cqw units.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container query should include a padding rule with cqw units. Check the syntax and placement.

steps.title: Add container-name to the container
steps.instruction: Add a container-name property to the .container rule and set its value to 'card-container'.
steps.hint: The container-name property allows you to give a specific name to your container, which can be referenced in container queries. Add it alongside container-type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The .container rule will have both container-type and container-name properties defined.
successCriteria: The .container CSS rule includes container-name: card-container;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a container-name property, but check the value. It should be 'card-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container-name property is missing or incorrect. Add container-name: card-container; to the .container rule.

steps.title: Create a named container query using cqh unit
steps.instruction: Add a new container query that targets the named container (using @container containerName) and sets the card's height to 10cqh when the container's height is at least 200px.
steps.hint: Use @container with the container name and a min-height condition, then inside it, set .card { height: 10cqh; }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The card's height will adjust based on the container's height using the cqh unit when the container is at least 200px tall.
successCriteria: A container query targeting the named container with min-height: 200px is added, and inside it, .card has height: 10cqh.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your container query uses the correct container name and includes height: 10cqh for the .card selector.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: you need @container containerName (min-height: 200px) { .card { height: 10cqh; } }.

steps.title: Combine cqw and cqh units for aspect ratio
steps.instruction: Inside the existing container query for the named container 'card-container', add a CSS rule that uses calc() with both cqw and cqh units to set the card's aspect-ratio property to maintain a 4:3 ratio.
steps.hint: Use aspect-ratio: calc(4 * 1cqw / 3 * 1cqh); or a similar calculation that combines both container query units.
steps.expectedOutcome: The card elements will maintain a 4:3 aspect ratio when the container height is at least 200px, using both cqw and cqh units in a calculation.
successCriteria: The named container query includes a rule for .card with aspect-ratio using calc() that references both cqw and cqh units.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your aspect-ratio rule uses both cqw and cqh units inside a calc() function within the named container query.
steps.feedbackWrong: The aspect-ratio rule should be added inside the existing @container card-container query, using calc() with both cqw and cqh units.

steps.title: Add media query for comparison
steps.instruction: Add a media query that uses vw and vh units to style the .card elements, creating a visual contrast with the container query units.
steps.hint: Use @media (min-width: 600px) to target larger viewports, then inside it, write rules for .card using vw for font-size and vh for padding.
steps.expectedOutcome: A media query is added that applies viewport-based units (vw, vh) to .card elements when the viewport is at least 600px wide, demonstrating the difference from container query units.
successCriteria: A media query with @media (min-width: 600px) is present, containing rules for .card that use vw for font-size and vh for padding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a media query, but it might not include both vw and vh units, or the viewport condition could be different. Check that your media query uses @media (min-width: 600px) and applies both vw and vh to .card properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: No media query with vw and vh units was found. Remember to add a @media rule that targets viewports at least 600px wide and styles .card using vw for font-size and vh for padding.

steps.title: Test responsiveness by adjusting container size
steps.instruction: Modify the .container CSS rule to add explicit width and height values,
steps.hint: Add width and height properties to the .container selector. Try values like width: 400px; height: 300px; to see the container query units scale.
steps.expectedOutcome: The container will have fixed dimensions, making it easier to observe how font sizes and padding change with cqw units when the container width changes, and how cqh units would affect elements when container height changes.
successCriteria: The .container rule includes both width and height properties with explicit values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you add both width and height properties to the .container selector.
steps.feedbackWrong: modify the existing .container rule to include width and height properties with specific pixel values.
